era_visual_canon.clothing: Mining era (1937-1966): miners and mill workers in sweat-stained cotton work shirts, khaki or navy shorts or trousers, leather work boots, felt slouch hats or cloth caps, often coated in fine dust, with little or no respiratory protection. Australian officials, inspectors and company managers in lightweight suits, ties and felt hats, or short-sleeved shirts in the heat. Migrant European and Spanish wives in simple cotton dresses, cardigans and headscarves. Children in shorts and cotton frocks, often barefoot or in sandals. Decline era (1970s-1990s): open-collar shirts, wide-lapel suits for lawyers and politicians, casual knitwear for retired former residents. Contemporary era (2000s-2020s): officials and lawyers in modern business attire; Aboriginal traditional owners and activists in casual shirts, jeans and broad-brimmed hats; any personnel inside the contaminated zone in modern disposable protective coveralls and respirators.
era_visual_canon.technology: Mining era: mechanical crushing and fibre-separation mills, belt conveyors, mill fans and early dust-extraction ducting, valve radios, wall-mounted telephones, manual typewriters, carbon copies, paper files, box and folding film cameras producing black-and-white or sepia prints, ceiling fans, basic hospital instruments including obstetric forceps. NO computers, NO digital displays, NO mobile phones, NO plastic signage, NO modern air-monitoring instruments. Decline era: 1980s office equipment, CRT televisions, landline phones. Contemporary era: modern legal and government offices, digital cameras, laptops, warning signage and permanent road barricades.
era_visual_canon.vehicles_machinery: Mining era: mid-century flatbed trucks and tipper trucks carrying ore and tailings, utility vehicles and four-wheel-drive bush vehicles, mid-century sedans, small propeller passenger aircraft landing on a dirt airstrip, ore crushers and conveyors at the mill, tailings dumped down gorge walls. Ocean liners from Málaga to Australia via the Suez Canal. Decline era: 1970s-1980s Australian sedans and four-wheel drives, demolition machinery. Contemporary era: modern four-wheel drives stopped at permanent barricades; no operating mine machinery.
era_visual_canon.interiors: Mining era: small worker houses and family homes of sheet metal, timber and asbestos-cement sheeting with plain furniture, enamel cookware, iron bedsteads and oscillating fans; a dust-choked mill interior with crushing machinery and thick suspended dust; a small town hospital ward with iron beds and basic obstetric equipment; government and company offices with typewriters, filing cabinets and paper reports. Later eras: family living rooms in Madrid with framed sepia photographs; courtrooms and parliamentary committee rooms; modern government offices.
era_visual_canon.forbidden_anachronisms: In mining-era scenes: no modern respirators, hazmat suits, hi-visibility vests or hard hats with modern logos; no sealed bitumen roads with painted lines; no modern four-wheel drives, SUVs or pickup trucks; no jet aircraft at the airstrip; no plastic warning signs or asbestos-hazard pictograms; no mobile phones, digital cameras, computers or LED lighting; no solar panels, satellite dishes or wind turbines; no contemporary clothing, sneakers or synthetic sportswear.
era_visual_canon.materials_textures: Worker houses built from corrugated sheet metal, timber and asbestos-cement sheeting; loose, crumbling fibrous asbestos that shreds into fine powder when handled; compacted asbestos tailings laid as the surface of roads, yards, driveways, the schoolyard, public spaces and the airstrip; fine powdery dust coating people, buildings and the mill; loose tailings dumps tipped into the gorges and washed by water into creek beds, pools and floodplains.
era_visual_canon.color_palette: Exterior dominated by intense red earth and red dust under harsh desert light, with blue-grey asbestos tailings surfaces and pale grey dust films over buildings and workers; interiors not documented; surviving family imagery described as sepia-toned.
era_visual_canon.scale_dimensions: A small, isolated outback mining town with a dirt airstrip sized for small propeller aircraft, three mines in the surrounding gorges, more than three million tonnes of tailings left behind, and an official asbestos management area of 46,840 hectares extending down drainage lines toward the Fortescue River.
era_visual_canon.distinctive_features: A small mining town in the red Pilbara desert whose own roads, yards, schoolyard and airstrip were paved with blue asbestos tailings, so the poison literally formed the ground people walked and played on; today it is an emptied, demolished, unmapped zone sealed by permanent barricades.
era_visual_canon.demographics: Documented workforce of Australian miners and mill workers, post-war European displaced persons assigned under federal work contracts (1948-1951), European recruits from private CSR recruitment trips (from 1950), and Spanish migrant families under the Spain-Australia migration agreement (early 1960s), with wives and young children living in town; mill workers dressed in dust-coated work clothes; Banjima Aboriginal traditional owners documented on their country in the contemporary era. Ethnicity and origin come from written records and testimony, not photographs.
era_visual_canon.visual_reference_availability: No sourced visual block was supplied; every place/object statement above derives from TEXT sources: oral testimony (red earth, dust everywhere, sheet-metal, timber and asbestos-cement houses, small propeller plane, children shredding asbestos), official and historical documents (tailings used for town, airstrip, roads, yards, schoolyard; mill dust clouds recorded by the Board of Reference in 1957; permanent barricades; water-borne deposits in creeks and floodplains), and technical reports (tonnages, 46,840 ha area). Family photographs are mentioned in text (portrait with bandaged foot, baptism photo dated 1963-07-07, sepia family photos in an interview) but were not provided. The blue-grey colour of tailings is INFERENCE from the documented blue asbestos (crocidolite); interior colours are undocumented.

condition_evolution.at_event: An operating mining town in the early 1960s: inhabited sheet-metal and asbestos-cement houses, a working mill wrapped in thick dust clouds, trucks dumping tailings to surface roads, yards and the schoolyard, children playing on the ground, and small propeller planes landing on the tailings airstrip.
condition_evolution.later: After mining ended in December 1966 the town was progressively reduced from 1978, its school, nursing post and police station closed and buildings demolished from 1986 to 1992, the airport closed in 1993, power cut in 2006, the town formally abolished and erased from maps and signs in 2007, the last residents gone by 2022-2023 and remaining structures demolished, leaving tailings eroding into creeks and the Fortescue catchment behind permanent barricades on every access road.

periods.clothing: Rough bush work clothes for prospectors and early miners: cotton shirts, braces, wide-brimmed felt hats, heavy boots; officials in wartime-austere suits and hats.
periods.technology: Small-scale hand and early mechanical asbestos extraction, basic crushing, valve radios, typewriters, paper inspection reports; no dust control beyond rudimentary measures.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Early mid-century trucks and utility vehicles on unsealed tracks, simple mine headings in gorge walls, horse-drawn or truck-hauled loads.
periods.interiors: Rough camps, tents and basic sheet-metal huts; spartan government offices.

periods.clothing: Dust-covered miners and mill hands in work shirts, shorts or trousers and boots; migrant families in modest European clothing adapted to heat; officials and doctors in lightweight suits or short sleeves with ties.
periods.technology: Full-scale crushing mill with conveyors, fans and later dust-reducing equipment, valve radios, telephones, typewriters, film cameras producing sepia and black-and-white family photos.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Ore and tipper trucks spreading tailings on roads and yards, small propeller aircraft on the tailings-surfaced airstrip, mid-century sedans and bush vehicles, ocean liners carrying migrants.
periods.interiors: Sheet-metal, timber and asbestos-cement houses, town hospital, school with tailings-covered yard, churches and community buildings, dusty mill interior.

periods.clothing: Remaining residents and visitors in 1970s-1980s casual wear; lawyers, judges and politicians in period suits; ill former workers in hospital gowns or casual clothes.
periods.technology: Landline phones, typewriters giving way to early computers in offices, CRT televisions, court and parliamentary paperwork.
periods.vehicles_machinery: 1970s-1980s sedans and four-wheel drives, demolition machinery removing town buildings, no mining machinery operating.
periods.interiors: Shrinking town with closed school, nursing post and police station; courtrooms, parliamentary rooms, migrant family homes in Madrid.

periods.clothing: Contemporary casual wear for Banjima traditional owners and activists; modern business attire for lawyers, officials and a UN rapporteur; modern protective coveralls and respirators for anyone inside the zone.
periods.technology: Modern warning signage, permanent barricades, contemporary offices and media equipment.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Modern four-wheel drives stopped outside barricaded access roads; no aircraft at the closed airstrip.
periods.interiors: Modern government offices, legal offices, interview settings with framed old family photographs.

people_groups.who: Australian prospectors and early mine owners who opened blue asbestos workings in the Hamersley Ranges gorges.
people_groups.appearance: Australian men of British or Irish descent, fair skin deeply sun-tanned and weathered, short hair, lean wiry build from bush prospecting.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Rolled-sleeve cotton work shirts, braces, heavy trousers, leather boots and wide-brimmed felt hats, sweat- and dust-stained from the desert.

people_groups.who: Managers and executives of ABA and its parent CSR, a Sydney sugar company with little mining experience, plus town steering committee members.
people_groups.appearance: Australian men of British descent, fair complexions, neatly cut and combed hair, office-worker builds.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Lightweight suits or short-sleeved white shirts with ties in the heat, felt hats, polished shoes; dark formal suits in head-office settings.

people_groups.who: Australian state mines inspectors, deputy mining engineers, public health doctors, a health commissioner, health inspectors and an industrial hygienist who reported on the dust.
people_groups.where_when: Wittenoom mine, mill and town and government offices, 1944-1968.
people_groups.appearance: Australian men of British descent, fair skin, short neat hair, professional office builds.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Wide-lapel lightweight suits, ties, felt fedoras, sometimes shirt sleeves with rolled cuffs during site inspections.
Narrower-lapel suits or short-sleeved shirts with slim ties, short back-and-sides haircuts, notebooks and clipboards on site.

people_groups.who: Asbestos miners, mill hands and fitters: Australian workers, post-war European displaced persons on federal contracts, European recruits from CSR trips, and Spanish migrants.
people_groups.where_when: Wittenoom mines, mill and town, 1937-1966, with a high-turnover workforce throughout.
people_groups.appearance: Mixed Australian (British-descended) and Southern, Central and Eastern European men, light to olive skin darkened by sun, short hair, lean muscular builds from heavy manual labour, often coated in fine dust.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Singlets or cotton work shirts, heavy trousers or shorts, leather boots, felt hats or cloth caps, no respiratory protection, everything grey with dust.
Dust-caked work shirts, shorts or overalls, hobnailed boots, cloth caps or slouch hats, occasional rudimentary cloth masks, slicked short hair after shifts.

people_groups.who: Spanish migrant miners' families from Madrid who came under the Spain-Australia migration agreement, including wives, infants and children, and their later adult children working in media.
people_groups.where_when: Ships via Suez and Wittenoom 1962-1964, Australia until 1971, Madrid from 1966 and 1971, an Australian airport in 1985, and later interviews into the 2020s.
people_groups.appearance: Spanish Mediterranean people with olive to light skin, dark brown or black hair, dark eyes, slim to medium builds; women and children tanned and dusted red in Wittenoom.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Women in modest cotton dresses, cardigans and headscarves with neat set hair; men in work clothes or a pressed shirt and trousers on Sundays; children in shorts, frocks and sandals.
Mid-to-late 1960s Spanish urban clothing: knee-length dresses, knit cardigans, men in suits or sports jackets, children in school uniforms.
1980s casual wear for adult children, such as jeans, shirts and jackets; parents in conservative Spanish middle-class clothing.
Elderly women in modest blouses and cardigans surrounded by framed photographs; adult children in contemporary casual or professional media attire.

people_groups.who: Children of miners, including Spanish migrant children, who grew up in the tailings-paved town and played with asbestos.
people_groups.appearance: Australian, European and Spanish children with light to olive skin, tanned, tousled hair, dusted with red earth and fine asbestos powder.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Boys in cotton shorts and short-sleeved shirts, girls in simple cotton frocks, often barefoot or in sandals, with hair cut short against the heat.

people_groups.who: Australian Workers' Union representatives, employer advocates and members of the arbitration Board of Reference who negotiated the dust allowance.
people_groups.appearance: Australian men of British descent, fair skin, short neat hair, mixed office and former manual-labour builds.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Union men in open-collar shirts and work trousers or plain jackets; board members and employer representatives in suits, ties and felt hats.

people_groups.who: Australian prime ministers, state premiers, ministers, parliamentary inquiry leaders and committee chairs dealing with Wittenoom.
people_groups.where_when: Canberra and Perth government and parliament settings, 1947, 1978-1994, 2016-2026.
people_groups.appearance: Predominantly Australian men of British descent, fair skin, short groomed hair, middle-aged office builds.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Double-breasted or wide-lapel dark suits, white shirts, ties, felt hats and brilliantined hair.
Wide-lapel then broad-shouldered business suits, patterned ties and side-parted hair.
Contemporary slim-cut business suits, open-collar shirts or ties, modern short haircuts.

people_groups.who: Former Wittenoom workers and residents with asbestos disease, the Asbestos Diseases Society of Australia, and the lawyers who litigated against the company and the state.
people_groups.appearance: Mixed Australian and European-born adults; ill former workers aged, thin and frail from lung disease.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Former workers in plain casual shirts and cardigans, some in hospital gowns; lawyers in 1980s broad-lapel suits.
Advocates and lawyers in contemporary professional attire at press events and offices.

people_groups.who: Banjima Aboriginal traditional owners, elders and members of BNTAC whose country includes Wittenoom.

people_groups.appearance: Aboriginal Australian people with dark brown skin, dark curly or wavy hair, elders with grey hair and beards, builds shaped by outdoor life in the Pilbara.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Casual collared or T-shirts, jeans or work trousers, boots and broad-brimmed hats on country; neat shirts or jackets for meetings and legal announcements.

people_groups.who: A visiting United Nations special rapporteur investigating toxic contamination.
